title: Looking Backward: 2000-1887
description: The most influential American utopia ever written: a Bostonian wakes in the year 2000. It is a prose fiction work of 1888 by Edward Bellamy; it belongs to American Realism and the Howells Program and it is catalogued here under Early Scientific Romance and Utopian Speculation; Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey and the record grades it as major canon.
plot_or_argument: Julian West, a wealthy Bostonian, falls asleep in 1887 and wakes in the year 2000 to find a cooperative commonwealth in which industry is nationalised, poverty abolished and the arts flourishing; his guide Dr Leete explains the new society, and Julian falls in love with the doctor's daughter.
narrative_structure: A novel in twenty-eight chapters, framed by the sleeper's awakening. A frame narrative in which the witness reports the machine, the society or the world, and the inventor explains his discovery in dialogue.
principal_characters: Julian West; Dr Leete; Edith Leete; Mr Barton; the citizens of the year 2000
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the scientific romance: the frame narrative of the witness, the set-piece description of the machine, the society or the world, and the dialogue of exposition in which the inventor explains his discovery.
historical_context: Boston in 1887, the labour unrest of the Gilded Age and the reform movements of the 1880s. The record dates the work as composed between 1887 and 1888 and first published in 1888 and the corpus places it within American Realism and the Howells Program, it is catalogued under early scientific romance and utopian speculation; social inquiry and the documented survey.
literary_significance: Looking Backward sold in the hundreds of thousands, founded the Nationalist movement and made Edward Bellamy a world figure: it created the mass readership for the socialist future and is the founding text of the American utopian novel, one of the most widely read books of the nineteenth century.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as E. Bellamy. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published by Ticknor and Company of Boston in January 1888, after the refusal of several publishers; more than a million copies were sold in the author's lifetime and the book founded the Nationalist clubs. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Caesar's Column: A Story of the Twentieth Century

A frame narrative in which the witness reports the machine, the society or the world, and the inventor explains his discovery in dialogue. A novel in chapters driven by heredity, appetite and environment, the accumulation of physiological and economic detail carrying the action to its determined end.
principal_characters: Gabriel Weltstein; Caesar Lomellini; the Brotherhood of Destruction; the Prince
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the scientific romance: the frame narrative of the witness, the set-piece description of the machine, the society or the world, and the dialogue of exposition in which the inventor explains his discovery. The author's characteristic manner is the future history narrated from a later age.

literary_significance: Caesar's Column is the great American dystopia of the 1890s and the direct ancestor of the twentieth-century anti-utopia: its vision of class war, the modern metropolis and the totalitarian mob made it a populist bestseller and a central text of the American protest novel.

title: Progress and Poverty
description: The most widely read work of economics of the nineteenth century: why poverty grows with progress. It is a prose work of 1879 by Henry George; it is catalogued here under Social Inquiry and the Documented Survey; Lecture and Popular Address and the record grades it as major canon.
plot_or_argument: George states the paradox that as wealth increases so does poverty, surveys the history of wages, rent and interest, and argues that the root of the problem is the private ownership of land, proposing a single tax on land value that would abolish poverty without confiscating capital.
narrative_structure: Ten books of economic argument, from the paradox to the remedy. A survey in chapters and sections, the case, the interview and the table set beside each other, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated evidence. The printed lecture: the address to the audience, the repetition and the triadic climax, and the peroration, retaining the shape of the delivery.
principal_characters: Henry George as author; the landowning class; the labouring poor
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the survey: the tabulated evidence, the interviewed voice quoted verbatim, the statistical paragraph and the argument from the case, with the reforming conclusion drawn from the accumulated document. The author's characteristic manner is the plain, forceful argument addressed to the common reader.
historical_context: The United States and Britain after the depression of 1873, the land question of Ireland and the emerging labour movement. The record dates the work as composed between 1877 and 1879 and first published in 1879 and it is catalogued under social inquiry and the documented survey; lecture and popular address.
literary_significance: Progress and Poverty made the single tax a world movement and was translated into every major language: it shaped the progressive and labour politics of Britain, America and Australia for a generation and is the most widely read work of economics of the nineteenth century.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Henry George (economist). No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1879, as prose (political economy), by Henry George. Composed between 1877 and 1879. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: The Damnation of Theron Ware

narrative_structure: A novel in three parts, from the arrival in Octavius to the collapse. A novel in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution, with the material world of the household described at length. title: History of Ireland: Heroic Period
description: The book that brought the Ulster cycle back into modern literature and started the Irish revival. It is a prose work of 1878 by Standish James O'Grady; it is catalogued here under Serial and Monthly-Part Novel; Idyll and Domestic Narrative Poem and the record grades it as major canon.
plot_or_argument: O'Grady retells the Irish heroic age from the Annals and the sagas: the coming of the Tuatha De Danann, the wars of the Firbolgs, the deeds of Cuchulain and the heroes of the Red Branch, in a prose narrative that made the Irish epic available to the modern reader.
narrative_structure: A history in two volumes, retelling the Ulster cycle. Continuous prose in sections or chapters, the argument or the account advanced from its statement to its conclusion.
principal_characters: Cuchulain; the Red Branch; Conchobar; the Tuatha De Danann; Queen Meave
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose: the argument or the account is carried in continuous prose, divided into sections or chapters. The author's characteristic manner is the retelling of the saga in Victorian prose.
historical_context: Ireland in the 1870s, the antiquarian recovery of the Irish manuscripts and the beginnings of the national revival. The record dates the work as composed between 1876 and 1878 and first published in 1878 and it is catalogued under serial and monthly-part novel; idyll and domestic narrative poem.
literary_significance: History of Ireland: Heroic Period reintroduced the Irish heroic sagas to the nineteenth century and was called by Yeats the founding book of the Irish Literary Revival: it made the Ulster cycle available to modern literature and gave the revival its heroic subject and its model of the national epic.

title: Cuculain and His Contemporaries

plot_or_argument: O'Grady retells the story of Cuchulain from his training with Scathach to his death, and the great cattle raid of Cooley, in a heroic prose that made the Tain Bo Cuailnge available to the modern reader for the first time.
narrative_structure: A narrative retelling in three parts, from the training to the death. A novel issued in monthly parts, each part carrying its own set piece and closing on a suspension, the parts gathered afterwards into the volume.
principal_characters: Cuchulain; Scathach; Ferdiad; Queen Meave; Conall Cernach
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the serial: the instalment-shaped chapter, the set-piece opening and the suspended close of each number, the recapitulation of the previous part and the plate or illustration marking the division. The author's characteristic manner is the retelling of the saga in Victorian prose.
historical_context: Ireland in the 1880s and the antiquarian recovery of the great Irish epic. The record dates the work as composed between 1879 and 1880 and first published in 1880 and it is catalogued under serial and monthly-part novel; idyll and domestic narrative poem.
literary_significance: Cuculain and His Contemporaries made the Tain Bo Cuailnge available to modern literature for the first time and completed the work begun by the Heroic Period: it gave the Irish revival its central hero and its great epic, and it is the source of Yeats's and Lady Gregory's Cuchulain.

bibliographical_notes: First published in 1880, as prose (saga retelling), by Standish James O'Grady. Composed between 1879 and 1880. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

plot_or_argument: The poems follow the Irish soldiers who left Ireland after the Treaty of Limerick to serve the kings of France — the Wild Geese — through the battles of the eighteenth century and into the exile, in lyrics of defeat, loyalty and the memory of home.
narrative_structure: A sequence of lyrics following the Wild Geese into exile. A collection of separate poems rather than a continuous narrative; the pieces stand alone and are commonly read individually.

meter_and_prosody: Verse. Verse: the line and stanza follow the conventions of the genre, and the poem is written to be read aloud. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the western landscape as the determining force.

literary_significance: With the Wild Geese is one of the great Irish historical poem sequences and Emily Lawless's finest poetry: its lyrics of the Wild Geese gave the Irish exile its permanent poetic record and made the Jacobite defeat a central subject of the revival.

title: Laurence Bloomfield in Ireland

title: The Half Sisters
